analysis.one_liner: Raises federal fines on automakers that violate motor vehicle safety rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised the maximum federal fine for a vehicle safety violation from $5,000 to $25,000 per violation, was referred to committee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the civil fines automakers face for violating federal motor vehicle safety rules — from $5,000 to $25,000 per violation, with even larger maximums for selling unsafe school buses — and would have applied those fines to anyone who causes a violation, not just the company that commits it. It was introduced in the Senate after the GM ignition-switch and Takata airbag recall controversies, when fines for hiding defects were widely criticized as too small to change behavior. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and passengers, including children riding school buses, would gain from safety fines large enough to change automaker math: with the old $5,000 maximum, a company could weigh a fine as a rounding error against the cost of a recall. Taxpayers and victims of defects would also gain because stonewalling federal defect investigations would become costlier per day.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, passengers, and school bus riders

how_it_helps.text: Raises the maximum civil penalty for violating federal motor vehicle safety rules from $5,000 to $25,000 per violation, making fines large enough to actually influence automaker behavior.
Increases the maximum penalty for selling noncompliant school buses or school bus equipment from $10,000 to $100,000, targeting safety rules for vehicles that carry children.

Raises to $25,000 per violation per day the penalty for refusing or failing to comply with defect inspection, investigation, and record-keeping orders, so stalling a recall investigation becomes more expensive.
Extends liability to any person who 'causes' a safety violation, not just the party that directly commits it, closing a way for responsible executives and suppliers to escape fines.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers and vehicle equipment makers would pay higher fines for safety violations and for refusing to cooperate with defect investigations, and executives or suppliers who cause violations could be newly liable. Some of those costs would flow through to vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: Higher per-violation caps only matter if regulators bring cases; the bill strengthens penalties but does not add investigators or speed up defect investigations, so its real-world effect depends entirely on enforcement.
Penalties are ultimately a cost of doing business that automakers can pass along in vehicle prices, so some of the burden could land on buyers rather than shareholders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — larger fines that make recalls cheaper than stonewalling — is real but modest: penalties apply only to violations NHTSA proves, and automakers could treat higher caps as a negotiating baseline. The main cost is that automakers could pass some penalty costs into vehicle prices, and critics of penalty increases argue safety is better served by faster NHTSA investigations than by bigger fines. On balance a reasonable, narrow consumer-safety measure that died without any recorded opposition or debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 22, 2014 and read twice, then referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation — its only action before the Congress ended.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded; the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and their suppliers are better off, since the higher fines and broader liability never took effect; no driver or parent gained anything from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

for.name: Sens. Edward Markey and Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsors of the bill at introduction.

for.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or committee vote was ever reported.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsors joined, and the bill never advanced past committee referral.

industries.note: The bill multiplies the maximum federal fines they face for safety violations and exposes anyone who causes a violation to liability. It died in committee, so they bear no cost.
Penalties for selling noncompliant school buses or equipment would have risen tenfold, to $100,000 maximum. The bill never advanced.
